sm: The Franklin Board of Mayor and Aldermen opened its Tuesday, November 24th meeting with roll call, an invocation and the Pledge. The mayor recognized Tennessee Kids Belong for the city being the first in Tennessee to offer foster-friendly businesses, with ninety-eight local businesses taking part. The consent agenda, items ten through sixteen, passed unanimously, as did the agenda as published. City administrator Eric Stuckey then announced a settlement of the consolidated federal lawsuit over the 2023 Franklin Pride Festival. It provides twenty thousand dollars in damages for each plaintiff and eighty thousand dollars in attorney fees, all paid by the city's insurer. That is about two and a half percent of the six and a half million dollars originally sought.

Stuckey said the settlement was the most responsible choice for taxpayers, that there is no finding of fault against the city, and that a separate lawsuit by Timothy Brown remains set for trial on January twelfth, 2027. The mayor then gave an update on the Lewisburg sidewalk project, saying the road will not be fully closed for the whole year, closures will be periodic for water line and storm water work, and the road can be reopened quickly if flooding occurs. Closures were pushed into January to avoid the December holiday season. Alderman Potts thanked staff and the Heath Place homeowners association for meeting quickly. The mayor also announced the Christmas tree lighting on December fourth at six p.m. with Matthew West, the Christmas parade the next day at one p.m., and wished Assistant City Administrator Walter Denton a happy birthday. The minutes from November tenth were approved.

The board held a public hearing on Ordinance 2026-18, the annual update to the zoning ordinance. Staff described changes since September. Gas station roofs stay pitched except in light industrial districts. Data centers were removed as a principal use in several districts but stay in planned development and light industrial districts, with a buffer of two thousand six hundred forty feet from residential lots, which staff called the strongest data center rule in Tennessee. Shipping containers would be allowed on non-residential sites if screened and on the ground. Staff also asked to remove a parking structure height item tied to the floodplain overlay, and one Patonsville Road property was removed from rezoning because it has been farmed since 1942. John Cooper of Holland and Knight spoke in support of the shipping container change for a Dick's Sporting Goods store. A motion to approve with that floodplain item removed was seconded, and then an alderman questioned the data center distance.

An alderman said a buffer of one and a half miles seemed too large, noting the existing data center on Carothers is under half a mile from Breckenridge but is screened by vegetation. Staff explained that the distance began at half of the proposed amount, was doubled after a board workshop, and was then doubled by the Planning Commission. Exceptions would have to go through the Board of Zoning Appeals, which would be hard because of strict criteria. Staff also clarified that the buffer applies to any new data center, even in a planned development, though existing data centers may expand. Because it is built into the use itself, a rezoning would not remove the requirement. If the distance were reduced to thirteen hundred twenty feet, it would not need to go back to the Planning Commission. Another alderman said nobody lives close to a site that is half a mile away.

An alderman moved to reduce the buffer to a quarter mile, but no one seconded, so the amendment died. The original motion passed unanimously. The board then passed Ordinance 2026-22, a zoning materials amendment giving more flexibility on metal and glazing for commercial recreation uses, with no speakers. Next was Ordinance 2026-31, creating a sewer camera inspection fee and a footage review fee, presented by Dylan Gaster of water management, to reflect a recent state law allowing third-party inspections. It also passed unanimously, as did Resolution 2026-94 on technical specifications for sewer inspection. The board then took up Ordinance 2026-27, rezoning twenty acres of planned development north of Mack Hatcher Memorial Parkway and east of Franklin Road, which is the Retreat at Iron Horse. A new resident spoke first, worried about construction facing her building.

Kelly Morris, a resident of seven years, said the earlier claim that forty percent of garages sit vacant is untrue, since people wait months or years for one. She said the project would remove thirty-six percent of rental garages, that the reserved parking spots offered could be nearly a hundred steps from her building, and that a three-story building would reduce light and privacy. She added that relocating renters does not erase the impact on those who stay. Richard Berg, speaking for over thirty-five residents, said they strongly oppose the plan and that the twenty-seven studios would rent for about sixteen hundred fifty dollars, roughly two hundred less than current one-bedrooms at eighteen fifty. He noted that city planning staff and the Planning Commission recommended denial.

Berg added that the mayor has publicly voiced his lack of support for the project. Michelle Nipp said the developer's promises, such as covering moving costs, felt unreliable, that the one comparable unit available had a poorly handled sewage leak, and that the project feels like a done deal. She also asked whether the preschool at the church, which would host construction staging, had been notified. No one spoke for the developer. Alderman Brown and Alderman Peterson explained that setting a public hearing date is not approval and urged residents to return and speak on January twelfth. The board voted unanimously to set the public hearing. It then unanimously approved contract 2026-046 with the Comptroller of the Treasury for annual written attestation, and the meeting was adjourned.
